text:
P arents of primary and secondary school pupils in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) have expressed concern over the ongoing teachers’ strike, warning that the continued closure of public schools could expose children to social vices and disrupt their education.
Abuja Metro recalls that teachers in public primary and secondary schools across the six area councils of the FCT embarked on an indefinite strike on Oct. 7 following a directive by the FCT chapter of the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC), led by Comrade Stephen Knabayi.
In a communiqué issued at the end of its State Executive Council (SEC) meeting held at the Labour House in Abuja on October 6, 2026, the NLC directed teachers under the Nigeria Union of Teachers (NUT) to withdraw their services over the alleged failure of the FCT Administration to address the vacancy clause and other outstanding demands.
Following the strike action, FCT Minister Nyesom Wike ordered the six FCT area council chairmen to enforce the “no work, no pay” policy against striking teachers and local government workers that failed to report to work.
Wike described the strike as politically motivated, warning that the administration would not tolerate such action.
Notwithstanding the directive, checks by Abuja Metro showed that learning activities across public primary and secondary schools in the territory remain grounded as teachers are yet to return to work.
Meanwhile, parents who spoke to our reporter on Monday expressed worry that the prolonged strike had disrupted their children’s academic activities, leaving many pupils and students at home without access to formal learning.
A parent, Mrs Hannatu Bawa, said the strike had deprived her children of the opportunity to attend school, adding that her two children in secondary school in Gwagwalada had remained at home since the industrial action began.
She said the children had taken advantage of the school closure to spend much of their time playing football rather than studying.
“In fact, the only time I see them is when they are hungry. The moment they eat, they sneak out of the house to play football instead of being in school. So, you can see the effect of the ongoing strike,” she said.
Another parent, Mr Gbenga Adekunle, a resident of Kuje Area Council, said the prolonged closure of schools had negatively affected his children, who now spend much of their time playing around the neighbourhood.
He said it was heartbreaking to see his children remain at home while their counterparts in private schools continued with their studies.
Adekunle urged the government to intervene urgently and address the teachers’ demands in the interest of parents and the future of the children.
“Sometimes, I have to go out looking for my children, including checking my neighbours’ houses, before they return home. You can see that we are in the political campaign period, and I am disturbed because I do not want these children to end up joining political thugs,” he said.
He called on the FCT Administration to prioritise education and resolve the dispute, warning that repeated strikes could undermine the quality and reputation of education in the nation’s capital.
“Let the FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike, prioritise the education sector in the territory. It is a shame that Abuja, which is the nation’s capital, is always experiencing strikes,” he said.
Similarly, Mr Ibrahim Abdullahi, a parent and resident of Kwali Area Council, said he could not afford to enrol his children in a private school, leaving them with no alternative but to remain at home during the strike.
He urged the government to prioritise the welfare of teachers, whom he said played a critical role in educating and preparing children for the future.
Abdullahi said he was disturbed by the sight of his children playing around every morning instead of attending classes, warning that prolonged idleness could expose them to antisocial behaviour.
“Everybody knows that we are in the electioneering campaign period, when there are cases of thuggery. Allowing these children to remain at home without being in school may seriously affect parents psychologically,” he said.
He appealed to the FCT Administration to address the teachers’ grievances and ensure that schools reopened as soon as possible.
Mrs Zainab Alhassan, a parent in Abaji Area Council, also expressed concern over the strike, saying it had forced her children to remain at home and disrupted their education.
She said the continued closure of public schools was taking a toll on parents, particularly those who could not afford private education, and warned that prolonged absence from school could have lasting negative consequences for children.
Alhassan appealed to the FCT Administration to urgently address the teachers’ demands to enable pupils and students to return to their classrooms.
The chairman of the FCT chapter of the Parents-Teachers Association (PTA), Alhaji Usman Abubakar, also raised the alarm over the impact of the strike, saying the continued closure of schools had exposed many children to activities that could jeopardise their welfare and future.
According to him, some children had resorted to hawking goods on the streets, while others were moving around in search of scrap materials since the strike began.
He added that the prolonged absence from school could expose children to antisocial activities, including political thuggery, and urged the FCT Administration to intervene by resolving the dispute with the teachers.
Abubakar said recurrent teachers’ strikes in the territory were damaging the image and standard of education in the FCT, particularly because Abuja serves as Nigeria’s capital.
He also warned that the situation could expose school-age girls to risks, including sexual exploitation and unwanted pregnancies.
“Today, several of our children are hawking all sorts of items on the streets, which may have adverse effects on the female child and could result in unwanted pregnancies,” he said.
The parents called on the FCT Administration and the striking teachers to urgently resolve their differences to enable children in public schools across the six area councils to resume academic activities.
